Data1 from the WHO adverse drug reaction database showed that cardiac events had been reported with the 5 most widely prescribed non-sedating antihistamines at that time (acrivastine, astemizole, cetirizine, loratadine, and terfenadine), and an attempt to quantify the risk2 suggested that use of these drugs was associated overall with a fourfold increase in likeli- hood of developing ventricular arrhythmias, although the abso- lute risk remained low. However, other centres3 have argued that definitive causality has only been proven for astemizole and ter- fenadine. In addition, a possible mechanism for drug-induced cardiac toxicity has only been found with astemizole and terfena- dine;4 both drugs have been shown to block cardiac potassium channels in vitro, a phenomenon that results in prolongation of the QT interval, which is a risk factor for developing ventricular arrhythmias. Studies5 with loratadine and cetirizine have found that neither drug blocked potassium channels in vitro, and a sim- ilar lack of activity might be expected with desloratadine and lev- ocetirizine; however, there is some evidence that mizolastine can block potassium channels at high concentrations in vitro6 (al- though a small study in healthy subjects noted no adverse effects on cardiac conduction at doses up to 4 times those normally giv- en).7 A case report8 of arrhythmias in a patient with pre-existing QT-prolongation given fexofenadine, did not appear to be asso- ciated with blocking of potassium channels.9 1.
